comment: Although the horse has bolted, I would ask that the public record more accurately reflect the creek's history and future state. Future dialogue, circulated material, on-line accounts, websites etc. should be mindful of the following: It’s inexact to say the planned diversion returns the creek to its natural condition, rather it returns it to an artificial man made post-mining era. Before the Judge Tunnel, the creek flowed freely through Old Town; along with other aquifers filled water troughs, numerous springs and supplied enough water to sustain year round wildlife, including abundant aquatic life. The intervention of a comprehensive diversionary pipeline creates the most significant artificial state this water course has ever been subject to. Empire Creek is a recent naming convention of unknown origin, as is the renaming of Deer Valley Creek to Silver Creek as shown at the recent public meeting. The Sanborn Maps of 1889, 1907 as well as the official survey of Park City Mines dated 1902 show the prominent blue waters of Silver Creek flowing via Empire Canyon through Old Town, while Deer Valley Creek joins it downstream. Distinctive hierarchy that emphasizes the importance of Silver Creek running through Old Town, alongside Main Street that’s supported by historic publications and first-hand “old timer” accounts. If the historic society could pin a rosette on a stream, then this would be the one it would do first…one could argue it's priceless, but also not worthy of the amount of money it now costs to return it to its true natural state– we should therefore question how did we let this happen?
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)

comment: I live in the Thaynes Canyon area and I am writing to object to the continued use of the area along Thaynes Canyon Drive as overflow parking for recreational users this winter. Many immediate neighbors share my objections. Mine are as follows: *The parking is contrary to the zoning of the golf course area as an urban park. The intent of this zoning is to preserve the entire golf course area as recreational and green space and to confine parking to the areas where it is intended (ie the Hotel Park City complex). The council should support the zoning that is in place, otherwise it is acting arbitrarily and against the interests of local residents in favor of largely out-oftown recreational users. *On a related note, the parking is a blight on an otherwise scenic recreational area that is a main feature of the neighborhood. *I understand that a long-term study is underway for this area. However, I also understand that an alternative option has been presented to contain the parking to the Hotel Park City complex this winter - this should be utilized instead of allowing parking that is contrary to zoning. *I noticed claims in the council papers that parking has occurred along Thaynes Canyon Drive for decades. That is not true from my experience. This has been a much more recent phenomenon and has accelerated during the Covid years, leading to objections by local residents. *Some neighbors immediately adjacent to the golf course area have said they prefer parking along Thaynes Canyon Drive than in their local streets. This doesn't indicate real support for the overflow parking - it is just indicating a preference for one form of illegal recreational parking for another. In addition to supporting the no street parking designation for Thaynes Canyon streets close to recreational areas and bus stops, the council should also enforce the proper zoning and prevent the overflow parking. *Aside from these points, the overflow parking represents genuine traffic congestion and safety issues in the winter months. People unload/load and mill around at the back of their vehicles right along Thaynes Canyon Drive, while cars drive past and often back-up waiting to turn on to Highway 224, particularly during peak times. I have a neighbor who drives the long way to/from her home because she is fearful of hitting children who might run out on to the road. This is already an area that presents safety concerns due to the pedestrian cross-walk, which is heavily used by golf and nordic users. I had a near miss recently with a teenager who leapt out into the cross-walk at the last minute to join his friends on the other side of the road. This issue is exacerbated in the winter with the icy road and unsafe camber of the road at the curve. As a final note, we should deal with this issue properly. Let's support proper longterm solutions, and not turn a blind eye to inappropriate band-aid solutions that pit local residents against recreational users.
source: eComment (written; published verbatim in council meeting minutes)
